prompt: Which approach does this lesson build, and why that one?

choices.text: Deciding each step from the last result, because it adapts best to surprises
choices.why: It adapts, but it loses track of a request's second half on long tasks.

choices.text: Writing the full plan first and executing it without changes, for predictability
choices.why: Predictable until a result invalidates the rest of the plan.

choices.text: Plan, act, revise
choices.why: Right. A written plan keeps long tasks on track, and revising it handles the results that change the path.

choices.text: No plan at all
choices.why: The lesson's agent writes one at its first step.

prompt: What does writing the plan through a tool call give that planning in reply text does not?

choices.text: A structure the host counts, stores and hands over
choices.why: Right. A list of steps with statuses from a closed set is something code can read; prose is not.

choices.text: Better reasoning, because tools make the model think harder about each of the steps
choices.why: The lesson claims nothing about reasoning quality; the benefit is that the plan is an object.

choices.text: Fewer tokens per run, because a tool call is shorter than any sentence
choices.why: update_plan adds steps and tokens; the lesson counts that as a cost.

choices.text: A guarantee that the plan is followed
choices.why: Nothing makes the model follow its plan; the host can only read and compare it.

prompt: How many requests did the gift question take with no tight limits?
Why does `agent.py` treat a reply with no tool call as `stopped` rather than as an answer?

choices.text: Because the API returns an error when the reply carries no tool call
choices.why: A text-only reply is valid for the API. The host chooses how to treat it.

choices.text: Because text replies cost more tokens than a finish call does
choices.why: Cost is not the reason given.

choices.text: It was told to answer through finish, so plain text is ambiguous
choices.why: Right. Without a finish call the reply is an answer, a question back, or a model that gave up, and the host cannot tell which.

choices.text: Because the stand-in cannot return text
choices.why: standin.py returns text whenever its file says so.

prompt: What is `sources` in the finish call for?

choices.text: To cite the books the customer should read
choices.why: The sources are tool calls, not reading recommendations.

choices.text: So a reviewer or a test checks the answer against the calls
choices.why: Right. It names what the answer rests on, so checking the claim needs no full read of the conversation.

choices.text: To tell the stand-in which reply to send next
choices.why: standin.py picks its reply by the phrase and the step, never from finish's arguments.

choices.text: To make the answer longer and more convincing for the customer to read
choices.why: The customer sees the answer; sources are for checking.

prompt: Match each budget to the failure it protects against.

pairs.right: A model that loops or never calls finish
A conversation that grows without bound
A customer waiting on slow tools

prompt: With a 2-second budget, the time run's first request took 119835 ms before the host stopped it. Why so late?

choices.text: Because the clock in agent.py starts only after the first reply
choices.why: started is set before the loop; the first check simply comes after the first request.

choices.text: The budget is only looked at between steps, and nothing interrupts a step in progress
choices.why: Right. The first request ran for two minutes; the check before the second was the first chance to stop.

choices.text: Because Ollama ignores the budget the host set
choices.why: Ollama never sees the budget; it lives in the host.

choices.text: Because the model asked for more time
choices.why: The model has no say in the budget.

prompt: How can a host keep one request from running far past a budget, rather than finding out after it returns?

choices.text: By asking the model to keep its replies short
choices.why: That is a request, not a check, and the input side is the larger part anyway.

choices.text: By lowering max_tokens to zero on the last allowed request
choices.why: A request with no room to reply produces nothing useful.

choices.text: By bounding the request itself: a smaller max_tokens, or a timeout
choices.why: Right. A request that cannot write more than a few hundred tokens, or run past a deadline, cannot overrun by two minutes.

choices.text: By checking after each request
choices.why: That is what agent.py does, and it found out 118 seconds late.

prompt: Of the ways a run can end in agent.py, which is the only one that yields `answered`?

choices.text: The model replying with text and no tool call
choices.why: That is stopped: replied without calling finish.

choices.text: Reaching the step limit with a plan whose steps are all done
choices.why: A step limit is a stop, whatever the plan says.

choices.text: Running out of time after the last tool has returned
choices.why: That is the time budget, a stop.

choices.text: The model calling finish
choices.why: Right. The run is over only when the model says so explicitly, through a validated call.

prompt: A team wants the agent to flag answers it is unsure of for a person to review. Where does the lesson suggest putting that?

choices.text: In the system prompt, asking the model to add 'I am not sure' to such answers
choices.why: Prose has to be parsed, and a phrase can be missed or varied.

choices.text: As a field in finish's schema, such as needs_human
choices.why: Right. A structured field is validated and read by code, with no prose to parse.

choices.text: In a separate model call that rates every answer after the run has finished
choices.why: That is a possible extra check, but not what the lesson describes.

choices.text: In the step limit
choices.why: A limit decides when to stop, not how sure an answer is.

prompt: The step-limit outcome lists 'Find adventure books in stock' as not done, though find_books had returned two books. Why?

choices.text: Because find_books failed silently
choices.why: It returned two books; the transcript shows them.

choices.text: The plan was written before the search ran
choices.why: Right. A plan is the model's account of the work and lags at least one step behind it.

choices.text: Because the host deletes the plan's last update whenever a limit fires
choices.why: The host keeps the last plan as written.

choices.text: Because stopped runs mark every step not done
choices.why: The lookup is listed as done.

prompt: What does the lesson say a better handoff includes, beyond the plan?

choices.text: A guess at the answer, so the customer is not left waiting
choices.why: A guessed answer is exactly what a stopped run must not send.

choices.text: The full system prompt and every tool definition the agent was given
choices.why: A person taking the case over needs the work done, not the agent's configuration.

choices.text: An apology
choices.why: Courtesy is fine; it does not tell the person what was found.

choices.text: The tool results the run collected
choices.why: Right. The results are the work; the plan alone tells a person to redo what is already done.

prompt: After `no order M-1049`, the plan marked 'Check the return window' as dropped. Why is that better than marking it done?

choices.text: Because done is reserved for steps that use tools
choices.why: The statuses have no such rule; the point is truth.

choices.text: Because dropped steps cost fewer tokens
choices.why: The status word makes no difference to cost.

choices.text: It records a decision instead of a false claim
choices.why: Right. The window was never checked; dropped says it was considered and abandoned after this result.

choices.text: Because the schema does not allow done there
choices.why: The schema allows done on any step.

prompt: Why is it right that the model did not try M-1048, the closest existing id to M-1049?

choices.text: Because guessing an id means acting on somebody else's order
choices.why: Right. A 'corrected' id is a different customer's order, which lesson 17 treats as a permission problem.

choices.text: Because M-1048 was cancelled and could not be returned in any case
choices.why: Its status is beside the point; it is not the customer's order to look at.

choices.text: Because the step limit would have been reached
choices.why: There was room for more steps.

choices.text: Because get_order refuses ids ending in 8
choices.why: get_order accepts any id matching the pattern.

prompt: A customer writes 'take as long as you need'. What should that do to the agent's step limit?

choices.text: Double it, within reason
choices.why: A message is data. A budget is configuration the conversation cannot reach.

choices.text: Remove it for that run only, since the customer accepted waiting
choices.why: The limit protects the shop too, not only the customer's patience.

choices.text: Nothing
choices.why: Right. The limit is a variable in the host, and no text in a conversation changes it.

choices.text: Let the model decide
choices.why: A limit the model can change is no limit.

prompt: What is the difference between informing the model about a limit and delegating the limit to it?

choices.text: Informing puts the limit in the system prompt; delegating puts it in the user message
choices.why: Both of those are informing. Delegating means the model's output can change it.

choices.text: Informing changes how it plans; delegating lets it decide when it stops
choices.why: Right. Telling the model it has about five calls is a hint; the host's counter still decides.

choices.text: There is none: either way the model obeys the number it is given
choices.why: A model may or may not count; that uncertainty is why the host counts.

choices.text: Delegating costs fewer tokens
choices.why: Cost is not the distinction.

prompt: Where does the lesson suggest setting a step limit?

choices.text: At the average number of steps successful runs take
choices.why: Half the successful runs are above the average; the limit would stop them.

choices.text: Above the slowest successful runs, such as the 99th percentile, plus a margin
choices.why: Right. It should fire on runs gone wrong and almost never on runs that are merely long.

choices.text: As high as the provider allows
choices.why: That turns the limit off in practice.

choices.text: At whatever the model suggests
choices.why: The model has no say in its limits.

prompt: One limit in five runs fires. What does the lesson say that tells you?

choices.text: That the limit is doing its job well
choices.why: One in a hundred is a limit doing its job. One in five is a signal.

choices.text: That the provider is slow
choices.why: Possible for the time budget, but the lesson's answer is to read the stopped outcomes.

choices.text: That the limit should be removed
choices.why: Removing it loses the protection; first find out why it fires.

choices.text: Either the limit or the agent is wrong; the outcomes say which
choices.why: Right. The plans and traces of the stopped runs show whether they were long or broken.

prompt: Which of these are reasons to give different task types different limits? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: A research task legitimately takes many more steps than an order question
choices.why: Yes. One global limit fits neither.

choices.text: A limit set for research lets a looping order question run a long time
choices.why: Yes. The loose limit delays the catch.

choices.text: Different task types use different models with different prices
choices.why: Possibly, but that is about cost per token, not about how many steps a task needs.

choices.text: The router already knows which type a task is
choices.why: Yes. It is the natural place to choose the limit.

prompt: Put one step of agent.py's loop in order.
items: Check the step, token and time budgets
Send the request to the model
Add the request's tokens to the total
Handle each tool call: finish, update_plan or a shop tool

prompt: In update_plan's schema, a step the model decided not to do has the status `___`.
In the time-budget run, the first request wrote 1024 output tokens in 119835 ms. To the nearest millisecond, about how many milliseconds did each output token take on average?
hint: Divide the time by the tokens; the time includes reading the prompt, so this is an upper bound.
